questions.q: Which term refers to a product's ability to remain functional in its environment?
options: Durability
Portability
Recyclability
Sustainability
questions.explanation: Durability is the design factor describing how well a product withstands wear and continues to function in its environment over time. Portability, recyclability and sustainability relate to movement, reuse and resource impact, not to remaining functional in use.

questions.q: What is the best way to evaluate a product's feasibility after design and prior to production?
options: Determine the price of the product
Make a prototype to test the product
Complete market research on the product
Examine the materials that are available for the product
questions.explanation: A prototype is a working model built before full production to test whether the design actually performs and is feasible to make. Pricing, market research and material checks inform the design but do not physically verify feasibility the way prototyping and testing do.

questions.q: A company designs a new logo for their product. What must the company do to protect their design?
options: Register a patent
Register a copyright
Register a trademark
Register a licence agreement
questions.explanation: A logo is a distinctive sign identifying a brand, so it is protected by registering a trademark. Patents protect inventions, copyright protects original creative works automatically, and a licence agreement grants permission to use IP rather than protecting the logo itself.

questions.q: The use of environmentally sustainable materials means that the materials are
options: biodegradable and affordable.
easy to be replaced and repaired.
re-useable or able to be recycled.
easily able to be renewed and replaced.
questions.explanation: Environmentally sustainable materials are those that can be renewed and replaced, ensuring resources remain available for future generations. The other options describe individual properties such as biodegradability or recyclability, which do not capture the renewable nature central to sustainability.

questions.q: What would be a designer's first step towards reducing the energy needs of a household?
options: Gather information on the cost of energy
Swap electrical devices for battery-powered devices
Explore the use of sustainable materials in developing user-friendly devices
Conduct research into the amount and timing of the household's energy consumption
questions.explanation: The first step in the design process is research, so the designer must first gather data on how much energy is consumed and when. Without understanding the existing consumption pattern, the other actions are premature solutions rather than informed design decisions.

questions.q: Why would an organisation authorise its research and development team to develop various 'concept' designs?
options: To redesign an existing good idea
To develop new and exciting future products
To rejuvenate an old idea that was never put into production
To ensure the research and development team maximise their use of new technology
questions.explanation: Concept designs are exploratory ideas created by research and development teams to envision and trial new and innovative future products. The other options describe reworking existing or old ideas, which is not the forward-looking purpose of concept design.

questions.q: Why is it important for a designer and the end user to communicate with each other?
options: To modify design ideas
To enhance brand recognition
To improve customer satisfaction
To collect feedback to promote further sales
questions.explanation: Communication between designer and end user ensures the product genuinely meets the user's needs, which improves customer satisfaction. The other options are narrower marketing or refinement outcomes that flow from, but do not capture, the central user-focused purpose.

questions.q: As new technologies are developed and released, existing products may rapidly become obsolete. What can designers do to address the waste caused by this cycle of obsolescence?
options: Use cheaper materials to reduce the price
Limit the functions of the existing products
Design products with components that are easily replaced
Restyle existing products to help maintain their market share
questions.explanation: Designing for easily replaced components lets users upgrade or repair parts rather than discard the whole product, directly reducing obsolescence waste. Cheaper materials, limited functions and restyling do not address the underlying disposal problem.

questions.q: Which of the following would be a key action when designing for social acceptance?
options: Review all processes and stages of a product's development
Use materials that are biodegradable or able to be reused
Consider environmental issues and production processes
Use innovative designs that are able to be disassembled and recycled
questions.explanation: Designing for social acceptance requires reviewing every process and stage of development so the product meets society's broad expectations. The other options each address only a single environmental aspect, whereas social acceptance demands a holistic life cycle view.

questions.q: How do entrepreneurs support the work of designers and generate value?
options: They create or expand economic activity by promoting new products.
They manage costs and gather research data for production of new products.
They take financial risks to promote social acceptance of innovative products.
They accept responsibility for design refinement and establishment costs of innovative products.
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurs generate value by creating or expanding economic activity, bringing designers' new products to market. The other options describe managerial or risk-bearing tasks that are secondary to the entrepreneur's core role of driving economic activity.

questions.topic: Design factors and success of innovation
questions.q: Why are some innovative products more successful than others?

criteria.descriptor: Provides reasons why some innovative products are more successful
Identifies a factor of success

questions.modelAnswer: Some innovative products are more successful because of the timing of their release, the designer's ability to address current trends, and how well they solve a real or genuine need. Other factors such as improved capabilities, ease of use and improved quality also affect the success of an innovative design.

questions.q: Describe how communication between members of a design team is supported by technology.

criteria.descriptor: Provides characteristics and features of how technology supports the communication between members of a design team
Sketches in general terms how technology supports the communication between members of a design team
Identifies or provides general information of how technology supports communication when designing

questions.modelAnswer: Improved capacity and capabilities of technology support communication between team members by allowing a greater volume and diversity of information to be shared quickly and conveniently from any location. Access to more information in a variety of formats speeds up the team's decision making, resulting in design solutions developed at a much greater rate and with more skilled people involved in the process.

questions.q: How does the use of sustainable materials and practices stimulate the development of innovative technologies?

criteria.descriptor: Discusses how the use of sustainable materials and practices stimulates the development of innovative technologies
Describes how the use of sustainable materials and practices stimulates the development of innovative technologies
Outlines how the use of sustainable materials and/or practices stimulates the development of innovative technologies
Identifies how a sustainable material and/or practice stimulates the development of innovative technologies

questions.modelAnswer: Using sustainable materials stimulates innovative technologies by pushing past the current limits of existing design options. Social acceptance of the need for sustainability encourages designers to explore additional alternatives and produce innovative solutions that use these technologies. The cyclic nature of the design process means designers keep exploring new sources and uses of sustainable materials, and experimenting, testing and exploring these possibilities further enhances the development of design ideas that incorporate innovative technologies.

questions.q: Explain why designers strive to improve upon their previous designs, even when the old products remain functional, easy to use and cost effective.

criteria.descriptor: Provides why and/or how designers strive to improve upon previous designs; shows a clear relationship between the improved and previous design/s
Discusses why designers strive to improve upon previous designs; shows a relationship between the improved and previous design/s
Describes why designers strive to improve upon previous designs; shows a link between the improved and previous design/s
Outlines why designers strive to improve upon previous designs
Shows some understanding of why designers strive to continue to improve upon their designs
Identifies an aspect of design improvement

questions.modelAnswer: Even when old products remain functional, easy to use and cost effective, designers keep improving on them because consumers readily take up newer, more innovative solutions that are easier and faster to use, more durable, better serviced or carry better warranties, or are seen as status items. Designers also take advantage of consumers' willingness to spend disposable income on new devices marketed to society's needs and wants, and of consumers' tendency to follow current trends and fashions. By making even minor improvements, designers can expand market share and profit and strengthen a product's image and branding, while taking advantage of new environmental advancements, innovative processes, techniques and materials that aid the marketing of their products.

questions.topic: Legal, ethical and technological factors and their impact on the success of innovation
questions.q:
The images illustrate a range of innovative products (a hoverboard, a drone and a driverless car).

Analyse the legal and ethical issues that need to be considered in the development of innovative products.

In your answer, you may refer to the images shown and/or other examples of innovative design.

Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate knowledge and understanding relevant to the question; communicate ideas and information using relevant examples; and present a logical and cohesive response.

criteria.descriptor: Shows a comprehensive understanding of the implications of legal and ethical issues in the development of innovative products; draws out and relates the implications; communicates using relevant examples
Explains the effects of legal and ethical issues in the development of innovative products; communicates using relevant examples
Describes the legal and ethical issues in the development of innovative products; may include a relevant example
Outlines a legal and/or ethical issue in the development of innovative products
Shows a limited understanding of legal and/or ethical issues

questions.modelAnswer: Designers carry both legal and ethical responsibilities when developing innovative products, and the hoverboard, drone and driverless car illustrate this clearly. Ethical issues include responsibility for safety while the product is in use, in storage or charging, and during production; environmentally questionable manufacturing processes and product life cycle implications; responsibility for manufacturing standards both locally and overseas; invasion of privacy (for example a drone's camera); affordability; provision of operational infrastructure; environmental impact; and the loss or creation of jobs. Legal issues include intellectual property; safety and the consequences of injury to the user or damage and injury to third parties or property; third-party insurance and licensing obligations; manufacturing standards; invasion of privacy; danger in public spaces on the ground or in the air; responsibilities for ownership and operation; interference with emergency services; policing of use; product warranty; and the management of operational infrastructure. A comprehensive response draws these implications together to show how legal and ethical considerations shape the success and acceptance of emerging technologies.
